articles.title: French budget and new elections in Spain
articles.heading: Nordic Alert
articles.fulltext:
Global key stories
French budget turmoil is putting pressure on the euro
, which yesterday reached its weakest level (1.12) against the dollar in 17 months. The French ten-year yield did not move much but remained near a high 4.9%, while both the US and German counterparts rose by a few basis points. The US ten-year yield reached its highest level in 24 years, with the price of oil (Brent) falling slightly to about
USD 100 per barrel. My colleague Bjarne shows in his 
analysis
 that the actual price - here and now - is instead around
USD 140 per barrel, as the price we usually see is what a barrel of oil costs a little further ahead in time
.
The unusual trend of both rising bond yields and stock markets in recent weeks continued yesterday. Technology stocks drove the stock market rise (Nasdaq, +1.1% and S&P 500 +0.7%). Chinese markets are closed today, but stock markets in Japan and Hong Kong are rising this morning. Futures point to positive openings in both Europe and the US today.
US services data 
gives a mixed picture. The ISM index stood at 54.9 in September and shows continued expansion, but at the same time does not paint as strong a picture of the economy as the services PMI. Activity slowed at the same time as input prices rose faster – a combination that keeps inflation concerns alive.
New elections in Spain
. Prime Minister Sánchez yesterday called new elections for November 29 after his minority government failed to get a housing package through parliament. Regular elections were supposed to be held next year, and the Partido Popular (PP) is leading in the polls and could together with the far-right party Vox reach a majority. Sánchez hopes that the housing crisis with high housing prices and housing costs will benefit the government, but corruption scandals within his own Socialist Party and the government's handling of the refugee crisis in Ceuta work to his disadvantage.
Keep an eye on France
. Today, the budget for 2027 is to be formally submitted. However, a first draft has already been presented with new savings of €43 billion. It is uncertain whether the parliament will approve the budget. Ahead of the 2027 presidential election, the hope is that the budget will show that France is on the right track and thus prevent the already elevated interest rate differential between French and German ten-year government bonds from spiraling further (read more 
here
 ).
The far-right presidential candidate Le Pen is speaking today and it will be interesting to see if she presents more details on her plans to save 125 billion euros over the next five years. All types of budget cuts in France usually meet fierce resistance. In recent days, over 5000 students have been arrested in violent protests against lack of resources.
Today's data calendar is thin
, but we keep an extra eye on German factory orders and industrial production for France and Spain.  
Nordic key stories
How the next Swedish government will look is still unknown.
 For those interested in politics, today's election (at 11.00 a.m.) of members of the Riksdag's committees may be interesting.

articles.title: Fransk budget och nyval i Spanien
articles.heading: Morning Alert
articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
Fransk budgetoro pressar euron 
som igår nådde sin svagaste nivå (1,12) mot dollarn på nästan ett och ett halvt år. Den franska tioårsräntan rörde sig inte särskilt mycket men låg kvar nära höga 4,9%, medan både den amerikanska och tyska motsvarigheten steg med några punkter. Den amerikanska tioårsräntan nådde sin högsta nivå på 24 år. Oljepriset (Brent) föll något till ca
100
USD per fat, men min kollega Bjarne visar i sin 
analys
 att det egentliga priset - här och nu - ligger runt
140 USD per fat, medan det pris vi vanligtvis ser är vad ett fat olja kostar lite längre fram i tiden
.
De senaste veckornas ovanliga trend med både stigande obligationsräntor och börser fortsatte igår. Teknikaktier drev börsuppgången (Nasdaq, +1,1% och S&P 500 +0,7%). Kinesiska marknader är stängda idag, men börserna i Japan och Hong Kong stiger nu på morgonen. Terminerna pekar på positiva öppningar i både Europa och USA idag.
Amerikanska tjänstedata 
ger en blandad bild. ISM-index uppgick till 54,9 i september och visar fortsatt expansion, men visar samtidigt inte lika stark bild av ekonomin som tjänste-PMI. Aktiviteten bromsade in samtidigt som företagens insatspriser steg snabbare – en kombination som håller inflationsoron vid liv.
Nyval i Spanien
. Premiärminister Sánchez utlyste igår nyval den 29 november efter att hans minoritetsregering tidigare misslyckats med att få igenom ett bostadspaket i parlamentet. Ordinarie val skulle ha hållits nästa år. Partido Popular (PP) leder i opinionen och kan tillsammans med ytterhögerpartiet Vox få majoritet. Sánchez hoppas att bostadskrisen med höga bostadspriser och boendekostnader ska gynna regeringen, men korruptionsskandaler inom det egna socialistpartiet och regeringens hantering av flyktingkrisen i Ceuta ligger honom i fatet.
Håll ögonen på Frankrike
. Idag ska budgeten för 2027 formellt lämnas in. Ett första utkast har dock redan presenterats med nya besparingar på 43 miljarder EUR. Målet att få ned budgetunderskottet till 5% av BNP har redan skjutits fram och kan bli svårt att nå även 2027. Det är osäkert om parlamentet kommer att godkänna budgeten. Inför presidentvalet 2027 är förhoppningen att budgeten ska visa att Frankrike är på rätt bana och därmed förhindra att den redan förhöjda räntedifferensen mellan franska och tyska tioåriga statsobligationer skenar i väg ytterligare (läs mer 
här
).
Ytterhögerns presidentkandidat Le Pen talar idag och det blir intressant att se om hon presenterar fler detaljer kring sina planer på att spara 125 miljarder EUR under de kommande fem åren. Alla typer av nedskärningar i Frankrike möter i regel motstånd. De senaste dagarna har över 5000 studenter gripits i våldsamma protester mot resursbrist.
Dagens datakalender är tunn
, men vi håller lita extra koll på tyska fabriksorder och industriproduktionen för Frankrike och Spanien.  
Sverige
Hur nästa svenska regering ska se ut är fortfarande okänt. Lars Calmfors, professor emeritus, skriver i en ledare i Dagens Nyheter att ett tillfälligt svar på regeringsfrågan skulle kunna vara en tjänstemannaregering (betallänk 
här
).
För den politiskt intresserade kan dagens val (kl. 11.00) av ledamöter till riksdagens utskott vara intressanta.

articles.title: Potential Democratic sweep and fiscal policy gridlock
articles.heading: US midterm elections
articles.fulltext:
President Trump’s weak approval ratings in the wake of the war with Iran and rising gasoline prices have increased the Democrats’ chances of regaining control of the House of Representatives. Opinion polls suggest that the Senate could also change hands. Trump would retain control over defence and trade policy and could veto Democratic legislative proposals. However, the scope for new fiscal policy reforms would be significantly constrained, while Democrats would gain greater leverage in fiscal negotiations. 
Key points
History points to a shift in the House
Both betting odds and polls indicate a possible Senate shift too
New congressional majority likely to create fiscal gridlock
Fiscal bargaining could lead to somewhat more expansionary policy
Presidential veto would block major policy changes
Appointments could be blocked if Democrats take the Senate
Tariffs rest on existing statutory authority
On 3 November, Americans will once again head to the polls, this time to elect all 435 members of the House of Representatives and just over one-third, or 35 of 100, members of the Senate. Republicans currently hold majorities in both chambers of Congress, a narrow one in the House at 219–214, with two vacancies, and a somewhat larger one in the Senate at 53–47. For Democrats to take control, they therefore need to gain only four seats in the House and four seats in the Senate, taking into account Vice President JD Vance’s casting vote. A prerequisite is also that Democrats retain their Senate seats in two states won by Trump in the latest presidential election, Georgia and Michigan.
History points to a shift in the House
The historical pattern is that the incumbent president’s party almost always loses ground in midterm elections, particularly in the House of Representatives. This has happened in 20 of the 22 midterm elections since the Second World War. The outcome in the House also tends to reflect developments in the president’s approval ratings and in generic congressional polling.
President Trump’s approval ratings have shown a clear downward trend, which has intensified since the US entered the war with Iran in February and gasoline prices rose. The share of voters who think Trump is doing a good job is now below 40%. Trump’s net approval rating – the share who approve of his performance minus the share who disapprove – is weaker than the lowest readings recorded during Trump’s first term as well as during the presidencies of Joe Biden, Barack Obama and George W. Bush. This also reflects the fact that Trump is a historically polarising president who evokes strong reactions among both supporters and opponents.
On the issues that matter most to voters, where Trump was seen as having the stronger policy platform ahead of the 2024 election – including the economy, inflation, foreign policy, immigration and crime – approval ratings are now clearly negative, particularly on inflation.
There is also a clear historical relationship between the average result in generic congressional polls – where voters are asked which party’s candidate they intend to support in their own district – and the number of seats each party ultimately wins. Democrats’ current lead of just over 8 percentage points is slightly larger than at the same stage ahead of the 2018 midterm elections, during Trump’s first term, when their lead was just over 7 percentage points. Democrats went on to gain 41 House seats in that election.
Most House seats are located in strong Democratic or Republican strongholds where a change in party control is unlikely. Redrawn electoral maps are expected to further limit the Democrats’ potential gains this time, with the net effect estimated to add roughly 10 House seats to the Republican side. The real contest is therefore expected to centre on around 40 seats, with more of them currently judged to lean Democratic than Republican. Polymarket betting odds currently indicate over 90% probability for a Democratic House after the midterm elections. Anything other than a change in control of the House would be a major surprise.
Senate outcome more uncertain
The Senate is more difficult to assess because senators serve longer, six-year terms. Most of the Senate seats being contested this year were last up for election alongside the 2020 presidential election, when Biden won, but the candidates are now facing an electorate that voted for Trump for president two years ago. Trump’s weak approval ratings nevertheless appear to be weighing on the Senate races as well, while controversial candidates have weakened their respective parties’ positions in some states – in Michigan and Maine for the Democrats, and in Texas for the Republicans.
Both betting odds and polls point to a possible Senate shift too
Betting markets now indicate a clear Democratic advantage in the Senate as well. This reflects improved odds in the states where Democrats are seen as having their best chances of gaining seats: North Carolina, Alaska, Maine, Texas, Ohio and Iowa. In Texas, a Democratic victory would mark the first time the party has won a Senate election since 1988. Republicans retain a slight advantage in Iowa according to betting odds, but the state is no longer viewed as being as safe for them as previously assumed. Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is considered to have very good prospects of retaining his seat in Georgia, while El-Sayed in Michigan has again strengthened his chances of defending the Democrats’ Senate seat there.
Opinion polls, based on RealClearPolitics averages, point in the same direction as the betting markets. Democrats are now ahead in all of the states listed above, including Iowa, although the margins are narrow in some cases (with Jackson (D) at a 0.1%-point lead vs Collins (R) in Maine). All of these states are now classified either as leaning Democratic or as toss-ups. Much can still change, however, with just over a month remaining until the election. Other states now also seen as toss-ups include normally reliably Democratic Minnesota and normally reliably Republican Nebraska and Kansas.
New congressional majority likely to create fiscal gridlock
What, then, would be the implications of a full or partial change in control of Congress? One of the most important consequences would be that the Trump administration could no longer pass fiscal policy reforms through Congress without reaching agreement with Democrats. Since Trump returned to the presidency, Congress has approved both substantial tax cuts through the Big Beautiful Bill in 2025 and around USD 70bn in support for immigration and border enforcement this spring.
Republicans have discussed the possibility of another package involving increased defence spending, while Trump has said he wants to send out new stimulus cheques to voters if Republicans win both congressional elections. The latter proposal, however, appears to have limited support even among Republicans, at least on the scale suggested by Trump – USD 5,000 per person – which would probably be even more costly than the combined support measures introduced during the pandemic and would significantly increase an already excessively large federal debt burden.
New debt ceiling negotiations?
If Republicans lose control of all or part of Congress, they will also need to negotiate with Democrats over raising the debt ceiling – the legal limit on how much the federal government can borrow to meet its obligations – once it is reached sometime next year. Such stand-offs have historically brought the US close to a self-inflicted default before the parties eventually reached agreement. One possibility, however, is that Republicans raise the ceiling before the next Congress takes office in January.
Fiscal bargaining could lead to somewhat more expansionary policy
As before, annual appropriations will have to be negotiated between the two parties, but Democrats would gain greater control over the process if they take one or both chambers. The scope for political bargaining would increase once Trump’s ability to pass new reforms is curtailed.
This could result in somewhat more expansionary fiscal policy if Democrats succeed in reversing some previously approved cuts, for example to health insurance programmes or food assistance, in exchange for additional defence spending. Control of the House would also give Democrats the speakership and therefore greater ability to bring their own legislative proposals to the floor. The risk of renewed government shutdowns during budget negotiations, similar to what happened last year, would remain regardless of the midterm outcome.
Presidential veto would block major policy changes
Trump would retain considerable control through his veto power, unless overridden by a qualified majority in both chambers. One objective for Democrats could nevertheless be to force some Republican lawmakers to take explicit positions on issues that may be popular among voters in their own districts.
For legislation outside fiscal policy, however, a qualified majority in the Senate – normally 60 votes – is generally required. One risk for Democrats is that voters become disappointed when it becomes clear that the party is unable to implement the policy reforms it has promised, potentially weakening support ahead of the 2028 presidential and congressional elections.
A Democratic majority in the House would also give the party the ability to launch new impeachment proceedings against the president or members of the administration. These would not, however, result in convictions unless Democrats secured the required qualified majority in the Senate, which remains unlikely.
Appointments could be blocked if Democrats take the Senate
If Democrats also win control of the Senate, they would gain the ability to block appointments to the administration, the Supreme Court and federal agencies such as the Federal Reserve. This would prevent Trump from appointing a successor to Jerome Powell when his term expires in January 2028.
Trump would still be able to appoint acting heads of departments and agencies – though not to the Supreme Court or the Federal Reserve – an option he has already used. Democrats would also gain control of Senate committees and the ability to hold hearings involving both political officials and external stakeholders, including businesses, for example in connection with allegations of corruption.
Tariffs rest on existing statutory authority
In foreign and trade policy, the president has considerable scope to pursue his own agenda. The tariffs introduced so far this year are based on existing statutes that allow the administration, following the necessary investigations, to take decisions without direct involvement from Congress.
President Trump’s increased control over federal agencies has also expanded the administration’s ability to alter regulations in areas such as the environment, energy and finance. In these areas, the main constraints on presidential power come not from Congress but from the courts, ultimately including the Supreme Court.

articles.title: Near-Term inflation above Norges Bank forecast
articles.heading: Norway 360
articles.fulltext:
Norway 360 – Weekly Market (Re)View Norway 360 provides you with a quick and broad overview of Norwegian macro, rates and FX. *** See attachment for full report ***
Macro highlights (I): Inflation to overshoot Norges Bank’s forecast near term  
After having surprised markedly on the downside in June-July, core inflation rose in August though being 0.3pp below Norges Bank’s estimate. 
Inflation data for September is due on Friday Oct 9. We estimate CPI-ATE to rise a notch to 3.1% y/
y,
 consensus expect 3.0% y/y while Norges Bank estimates 2.9% y/y. See our inflation preview 
here
.
The downward revision to Norges Bank’s near-term trajectory (by 0.5pp) in its Sep26 MPR was surprisingly large. Hence, we see a clear risk that CPI-ATE inflation will surprise on the upside in the coming months, which will underpin current market pricing of a 60% chance for a hike by December.
We reiterate that we believe more is needed for Norges Bank to deliver another rate hike; last year’s two rate cuts have now been reversed, and the Committee is clearly divided on what’s deemed as a sufficiently restrictive policy. In the end, long-term inflation drivers will be decisive.
The outlook over the next 12-18 months is mixed. A stronger NOK is expected to exert downward pressure but 
high wage
 inflation contributes to core inflation slowing only gradually. We see slightly higher core inflation than Norges Bank in the near-term, but slightly lower inflation later in 2027.
Macro highlights (II): Fiscal policy will remain expansionary in 2027  
The government’s budget proposal for 2027 will be presented on Wednesday, with key market data released already at 8.00 CET. 
There have been frequent budget leakages in media, pointing to higher spending on defense, child welfare, employment and crime prevention. Meanwhile, no major budget cuts have been announced. This point to an increase in petroleum revenue spending. 
The value of GPFG has increased further, up by approx. NOK 800bn from an estimated NOK 21258bn in the revised 2026 budget. This increases the fiscal leeway with NOK 24bn given the 3% fiscal policy rule.
The structural non-oil deficit is always covered via a transfer from the GPFG, as issuance of government bonds is only allowed for funding of government lending schemes and to cover maturing existing debt. 
The underlying borrowing requirement has been trending higher in recent years, reflecting both increased net lending and higher refinancing needs. The 2026 budget implied a borrowing need of NOK 96bn, while Norges Bank aimed at NOK 100-110bn to build up the cash reserve. We expect stable gross supply around NOK 110bn in 2027.
Rates highlights (I): 
Sticking with NOK STIR front 
steepener
 & flattener further out (‘broken fly’)
NOK curve is too linear out to the 1Y1Y point. 
There should be elevated risk for hikes to extend into Q1 (assuming very low chance of cut in this window), while beyond that the curve should be able to price deeper inversion if we get an energy disinflation impulse. Comparing to the AUD curve is interesting given that it is also a high yielder and arguably close to the rate peak.
Rates highlights (II): 
Buy NGBs on ASW as a risk-off hedge?
Norway’s outstanding fiscal position should underpin NGBs as a quality haven, especially in a bond crisis centered on Europe (politics, government spending, energy). 
However, relative ASW spread performance suggests NGBs have not yet attracted 
safe haven
 demand; the NGB 10Y ASW has been range-bound between 0-10bps since June, despite the move higher in rates.
There are two plausible explanations for this:
Positioning in NGBs are dominated by foreigners and mainly leveraged accounts which have been long ASWs. A deepened bond sell off risks triggering a further unwinding of positions.
The global bond sell-off needs to intensify and debt repayment considerations increase (as in 2012), to attract real money 
safe haven
 demand.
Despite the NGB 10Y ASW lagging peers as Sweden, positioning and muted activity from domestics suggest it is too early to buy NGBs on ASW as a risk-off hedge. 
FX highlights: 
Crowded NOKSEK longs look exposed to energy-led disinflation impulses
Upcoming data & events:
The trend in manufacturing production is moderately positive, while manufacturing sentiment remains 
lacklustre
. The split among petroleum-related manufacturing and traditional-manufacturing persists and is expected to remain ahead.
Government budget proposal for 2027 will be presented on Wednesday at 10 CET, but market-sensitive data will be released already at 8 CET. There have been unusually frequent leakages ahead of the budget, pointing to higher spending on defense, child welfare, employment and crime prevention. Further growth to the GFPG allows for higher fiscal spending within the 3% fiscal policy rule. 
Inflation data for September on Friday will be very important for markets. CPI-ATE is likely to surprise somewhat on the upside relative to Norges Bank’s near-term forecast, as it revised its near-term inflation projection significantly lower in its Sep MPR. The bank now expects CPI-ATE to edge 0.1ppt lower to 2.9% y/y, while we have a 0.1ppt increase to 3.1% y/y in our forecast.

articles.title: The price of crude oil in Europe today is $140/b
articles.heading: Crude oil comment
articles.fulltext:
Last week's oil price action distorted by rolling of the November contract last week.
 The December Brent crude oil contract rose $4.8/b, or 5% last week. Much of that gain was due to the roll-yield as the November contract rolled off as the M1 contract to be replaced by the Dec-26 contract. The backwardation between the Nov and the Dec contract averaged $6.5/b over the last three days before 1 October and the rolling of contract. The "gain" over the week was thus not much of a gain at all. If we just look at the M1 contract it instead fell 2% Friday to Friday though that disguises the change in the underlying contract over the week. The Brent M1 contract closed the week at $102.25/b. The announcement of 100 mb of oil from G7 SPR helped to ease prices at the end of last week. Though that effect seems to have faded today.
More barrels from Strategic Petroleum Reserves or really barrels which were supposed to be released previously? Nonetheless, Trump seems to be content and is backing down from diesel export ban.
 Trump threatened the world, but especially Europe with a US diesel export ban unless Europe agreed to release diesel from strategic reserves. G7 last week decided to release 100 million barrels of oil from strategic reserves. But here the obscurity starts. How much of that will be diesel? "Substantial release of diesel within 20 days" was the statement. If it happens late in this 20 day period, it would bring us very close to the US midterm elections which of course is what Trump is worried about here. IEA members promised to release 425 mb of oil from strategic reserves of which 125 mb was to be oil products. But a significant portion of that was never really released. The question is thus whether these "new" 100 mb release will really be new or if the lion's share of the "new" 100 mb is really just part of the old 425 not yet fully released. Well, it looks like the promise, irrespectively what it really is, has averted a US diesel export ban for now. And it did also help to ease prices a bit at the end of last week. An effect which looks like it has mostly faded this Monday.
$140/b is the price of crude oil in Europe today. 
Back to the complete distortion of oil and product prices in time and geography. The Dated Brent "spot" price averaged $123.3/b last week. But that is really the average Day_10 to Day_20 of the "daily Dated Brent" forward curve. But since this curve is in very steep backwardation, the real prices for physical oil cargoes at the very front-end of this daily curve sits well above the average of this daily curve. The physical premiums for Oseberg and for Fortis crude takes this steep backwardation into account. The full price average for Oseberg and Fortis last week were thus $142.5/b and $140.2/b. That is way, way higher than both the Dated Brent "spot" price last week and the average of the Brent futures price, the M1 contract, which averaged $103.2/b last week and is trading at $102.4/b
Extreme prompt tightness may fade or get much worse.
 The extreme prompt tightness and backwardation we see in the market today is a display of today's prompt situation and not necessarily a guide for the future. The much more relaxed Brent M1 contract (today December) at $102.4/b is maybe a reflection of an oil market either betting or expecting that today's problems will be resolved somehow over the coming three months. Or, that the current flow of oil out of the SoH at 17.5 mb/d (close to normal) will be sustained or even increase over time. But we don't know exactly why the flow of crude, products and LNG out of the SoH has been able to sustain at around 17.5 mb/d since mid-September (it seems). Is it because shippers are better at managing the risk or more willing to take the risk of transiting? Is it because the US military assistance is better? Or is it because Iran is paid by exporters and is allowing exports out through the SoH? It seems plausible that Iran expects the US to attack again after the US midterm elections. If so, then Iran may engage with fresh attacks before that date. Physical crude in Europe today is $140/b, or 2x the "normal" price of $70/b. But if tightness escalates further, then price of crude in Europe could go to 3x, 4x or even 5x the normal level. Let's hope that the US is able to keep the SoH "open" at a rate of 17.5 mb/d and that another 100 mb of oil from G7 helps to shield against that upside risk.
The global oil-stock cushion is getting "scarily thin".
 Looking at the Brent M1 Dec-26 contract, one gets the impression that risks may be fairly contained. Looking at physical spot prices in Europe however of around $140/b, the sense of stress rises substantially. The latter better reflects Amin Nasser, CEO of Saudi Aramco, when he recently said that the cushion capacity of global oil stocks are getting "scarily thin".
Some key questions helping to keep the Brent M1 price above $100/b:
 Will Iran initiate fresh attacks before the US midterm elections? Will the US attack Iran after the elections? Will the US be able to keep the SoH close to open at 17.5 mb/d? Will the Houthis re-attack the Saudi east-west pipeline and ships trying to traverse the Bab-el Mandeb Strait as the Saudi-backed Yemen government tries to retake areas along the Red Sea recently taken by the Houthis? How far will this have to go before China finally decides to step in as a peacemaker in ME negotiations?
ARA Crude oil, diesel and nat gas prices in USD/boe 
Source: SEB calculations and graph, Bloomberg data
Physical crude oil premiums for Fortis and Oseberg in the NSea in USD/b premium over the Dated Brent index
Source: SEB graph, Bloomberg data feed, Platts data

articles.title: Existing home prices rose moderately
articles.heading: Norwegian home prices
articles.fulltext:
Existing home prices rose somewhat more than expected in Sep, rising 0.3% m/m (SA), after the surprising 0.8% m/m rebound in the previous month. The September data exceeded Norges Bank’s monthly projection by 0.2ppt but is in line with our own estimate. The large regional differences in the Norwegian housing market continues to pull in opposite directions, although the differences have abated since summer. Higher mortgage rates and weak confidence weigh on demand, although being partly offset by still-tight supply. All in all, Today’s robust figures should not alter Norges Bank’s broader view on domestic demand, and we consider its annual estimate of 3.0% to be fair.
Details: 
Existing home prices fell 0.7% m/m in September, implying a 0.3% seasonal-adjusted rise. The year-on-year rate thus remains positive at 2.4%, and prices so far this year have risen 4.2%. Price momentum, as measured by the 3m/3m rate, slowed in early 2026 and remains at broadly neutral levels in September. 
In Oslo, prices rose 0.1% m/m (SA) and the broader picture of the capital remains weak in terms of price momentum. So far this year prices are down 0.7% YTD y/y. Should prices continue this way towards the end of the year, price growth will likely be negative between 1 to 3%. The large supply side has translated into especially weak price growth in the capital. At the same time, prices in Trondheim and Tromsø have seen very strong housing markets so far this year with prices rising 1.0% m/m and 1.5% m/m in September, and with YTD growth 5.1% and 12.2% YTD respectively. 
Supply of existing homes approved for sales fell somewhat in September (10.804) being 4.2% lower compared to a year ago. At the same time, turnover of existing homes rose (10.491), and were 5.8% lower compared to a year ago. The demand-supply balance thus indicates a 
balanced housing market
. In terms of housing turnover, average transaction time declined further to 48 days, which is in line with the long-term average. 
Housing starts picked up in late 2025, but new home sales have since plummeted, delaying the recovery in developer sentiment and the supply side. Although housing starts have risen modestly since before the summer, the 3m/3m rate remains at depressing levels. Combined with elevated building and material costs, this will continue to weigh on new home supply.
The 
growth in number of completed new homes 
has
 been on a steady decline since 2018
 and has dropped significantly in the past two years. A relatively stable 
situation for household formation
at the same time contributes to accumulating a structural deficit. To wit, the deficit has also shown up in the increasing rental 
prices which will absorb some of the underbuilt. 
Implications Norges Bank:
 Existing home prices rose by 0.3% m/m (SA) in Sep, 0.2ppt higher than Norges Bank’s own monthly projection. Its downward revision of its annual estimate was not surprising given large downside surprises for a number of months, now seeing full-year growth at 3.0% y/y in 2026. Large regional differences have been pulling in opposite directions, with Oslo being the weakest market this year and some west-coast region seeing the strongest price growth. Nevertheless, the accumulated undersupply of homes will provide a significant tailwind to price growth once mortgage rates come down. Norges Bank sees quite hefty price growth in the years to come, with accumulated price rise of 16.9% in 2027-2029. Overall, today’s figures are broadly in line with Norges Banks view of the housing market, and the lack of new build supply continues to lift demand into existing homes.

articles.title: Calm start to the week after a turbulent Friday
articles.heading: Nordic Alert
articles.fulltext:
Global key stories
Weak US labor market
 on Friday provided support to the world's stock markets and the S&P closed at +0.7%, despite a slight slowdown on Friday evening. It is mostly up in Asia (Nikkei +2.4%) and stock market futures point to small movements initially.
Not so many international statistics during the week, but minutes from the Fed and the ECB may be able to give some small clues about interest rate policy in the autumn.
 The market has lowered the probability of interest rate hikes in October to very low levels for both the Fed and the ECB and is also starting to hesitate a bit about a hike later this year, although the probability of an interest rate hike at the end of the year is still very high. Signals of both inflation and growth in the near term are mixed, as illustrated by the weak employment development in September (read more 
here
). Expectations of interest rate hikes during the autumn and winter were lowered and the probability of a hike in October is now only 15-20%. In addition to low employment and higher unemployment, wage growth continued to slow to historically low levels. Interesting for the inflation rate, although Fed Governor Warsh for some unclear reason played down the importance of wages for inflation.
The right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro 
(son of Jair Bolsonaro) won the first round of the presidential election in Brazil with 47% of the vote against 45% for incumbent president Lula da Silva (left). The second round will take place on October 25 and according to Polymarket, the probability of Bolsonaro becoming the new president has increased to 83% from about 60%.
The turbulence in the fixed income market continues 
and after a volatile day, European yields closed just over 5 basis points lower. The interest rate margin between France and Germany closed unchanged after increasing by 20 basis points earlier on Friday. However, US yields increased by 10 basis points during the evening.
Nordic key stories
Norway's CPI-ATE is expected to rise by 3.1%,
which is one-tenth higher than in August and two-tenths higher than Norges Bank's forecast. Norges Bank lowered its forecast for the CPI-ATE by half a percent for the next few months. We see upside risks in the short term, although we are a little more optimistic further ahead. Our assessment is that Norges Bank – with a policy rate of 4.50% – has now made a clear hike.    
A lot of Swedish statistics will be published during the week, and the flash estimate for the CPI is of course the most interesting. 
 Our forecast is that the CPIF excluding energy will increase from 0.5% to 0.7% in September, which is in line with consensus and the Riksbank. A weaker krona and indirect effects from energy indicate that inflation will rise gradually, but so far there are no clear signs of higher core inflation in either Swedish or international indicators. Prices for package holidays, hotels and car rentals rose more than usual during the summer and could fall back a little more than usual in September, which is a downside risk to our forecast. On Friday, growth data for August will be published, and strong sentiment indicators point to a clear upward rebound, after slightly weak figures in July. The momentum for growth appears to have strengthened in the third quarter, but high energy prices and higher interest rates suggest that the outlook going forward is not as bright. According to our assessment, CPIF inflation will rise to 1.6% in September, and the combination of high world market prices and the reversal of tax cuts on fuel means that inflation looks set to rise to 2.5% towards the end of the year. It remains to be seen how the ultimately slightly more optimistic households will react to a new cost shock. The Riksbank's interest rate hikes will push up total CPI inflation to 2.5-3% in 2027, which suggests clear downside risks for our optimistic GDP forecast for 2027.
SEB's Housing Price Indicator, which was published this morning, rises by 2 points to 43
. The indicator has been fairly stable in 2026 at relatively high levels and our forecast – that house prices will rise by 5% this year – seems to be on track. Early and larger expected interest rate hikes from the Riksbank are a downside risk for house prices in 2027. Mäklarstatistik presents house prices for August on Thursday. More about our indicator 
here.
Attempts to form a new Swedish government are continuing, 
but the conditions for a red-green government so far look uncertain. The Center Party has invited the Social Democratic Party, the Liberal Party, and the Green Party to a joint situation review on Friday, but at the same time sticks to its red line of not being in the same government as the Left Party. The Center Party, Magdalena Andersson, is to report the results of its soundings to the Speaker by October 12, but can request more time if meaningful talks are still ongoing. The Speaker has said that a vote on the prime minister will be held when the exploratory mission is completed. 
Stora Coop is reducing the prices of 600 of its best-selling products
 by an average of 6.5% nationwide. This is at least another sign that competitive pressure in the grocery trade is high and does not provide any support for any broad new price increase for food right now.

articles.title: Lugn veckostart efter svängig fredag”
articles.heading: Morning Alert
articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
Svag amerikansk arbetsmarknad
 gav i fredags gav stöd till världens börser och S&P stängde på +0,7%, trots en viss avmattning under fredagskvällen. Det är mestadels upp i Asien (Nikkei +2,4%) och börsterminerna pekar på små rörelser inledningsvis.
Inte så mycket internationell statistik under veckan men protokoll från Fed och ECB kanske kan ge lite små ledtrådar om räntepolitiken under hösten.
 Marknaden har dragit ned sannolikheten för räntehöjningar i oktober till mycket låga nivåer för både Fed och ECB och börjar även tveka lite om en höjning senare i år, även om sannolikheten för en räntehöjning för årsskiftet fortfarande är mycket hög. Signalerna om både inflation och tillväxt under närmaste tiden spretar vilket illustreras av den svaga sysselsättningsutvecklingen under september (läs mer 
här
). Förväntningarna på räntehöjningar under hösten och vintern skruvades ned och sannolikheten för en höjning i oktober är nu bara 15-20%. Förutom låg sysselsättning och högre arbetslöshet fortsatte lönetillväxten att avta till historiskt sett låga nivåer. Intressant för inflationstakten, även om Fed-chefen Warsh av lite oklar anledning spela ned lönernas betydelse för inflationen.
Höger-kandidaten Flavio Bolsonaro (son till Jair Bolsonaro) vann första rundan av president valet i Brasilien med 47% av rösterna mot 45% för sittande presidenten Lula da Silva (vänster). Andra rundan äger rum den 25:e oktober och enligt Polymarket har sannolikheten ökat för att Bolsonaro blir ny president till 83% från ungefär 60%.
Turbulensen på räntemarknaden fortsätter 
och efter en svängig dag stängde de europeiska räntorna drygt 5 räntepunkter lägre. Räntemarginalen mellan Frankrike och Tyskland stängde oförändrad efter att ha ökat med 20 räntepunkter tidigare under fredagen. USA-räntorna vände dock upp med 10 punkter under kvällen.
Norges KPI-JAE förväntas stiga med 3,1%
 vilket är en tiondel högre än i augusti och två tiondelar högre än Norges Banks prognos. Norges Bank sänkte sin prognos för KPI-JAE med en halv procent för de närmaste månaderna. Vi ser uppåtrisker på kort sikt även om vi är lite mer optimistiska längre fram. Vår bedömning är att Norges Bank – med en styrränta på 4,50% – nu har höjt klart.  
Sverige
En hel del statistik publiceras under veckan och snabbestimatet för KPI är naturligtvis mest intressant. 
Vår prognos är att KPIF exkl. energi ökar från 0,5% till 0,7% i september, vilket är i linje med konsensus och Riksbanken. Svagare krona och indirekta effekter från energi talar för att inflationen stiger gradvis men än så länge syns inga tydliga tecken på högre kärninflation i vare sig svenska eller internationella indikatorer. Priserna på paketresor, hotell och biluthyrning steg mer än vanligt under sommaren och skulle kunna falla tillbaka lite mer än vanligt i september, vilket är en nedåtrisk för vår prognos. På fredag publiceras tillväxtdata för augusti och starka sentimentsindikatorer talar för en tydlig rekyl uppåt, efter lite svaga siffror i juli. Momentum för tillväxten ser ut att ha förstärkts under tredje kvartalet, men höga energipriser och höjd ränta talar för att utsikterna framåt är inte lika ljusa. KPIF-inflationen kommer enligt vår bedömning stiga till 1,6% i september och kombinationen av höga världsmarknadspriser och reversering av skattesänkningar på drivmedel gör att inflationen ser ut att stiga till 2,5% under slutet av året. Det återstår att se hur de till sist lite mer optimistiska hushållen kommer reagera på en ny kostnadschock. Riksbankens räntehöjningar kommer att driva upp den totala KPI-inflationen till 2,5-3% under 2027 vilket talar för tydliga nedåtrisker för vår optimistiska BNP-prognos 2027.
SEB:s Boprisindikator, som publicerades nu på morgonen, stiger med 2 enheter till 43
. Indikatorn har varit ganska stabil under 2026 på relativt höga nivåer och vår prognos – att bostadspriserna stiger med 5% i år – ser ut att vara på spåret. Tidiga och större förväntade räntehöjningar från Riksbanken är en nedåtrisk för bostadspriserna under 2027. Mäklarstatstik presenterar bostadspriser för augusti på torsdag. Mer om vår indikator 
här.
Försöken att bilda en ny regering fortsätter, 
men förutsättningarna för en rödgrön regering ser än så länge osäkra ut. Centerpartiet har bjudit in S, V och MP till en gemensam lägesgenomgång på fredag, men håller samtidigt fast vid sin röda linje att inte sitta i samma regering som Vänsterpartiet. Centerpartiet Magdalena Andersson ska redovisa resultatet av sina sonderingar till talmannen senast den 12 oktober, men kan begära mer tid om meningsfulla samtal fortfarande pågår. Talmannen har sagt att en statsministeromröstning ska hållas när sonderingsuppdraget är avslutat. SvD
Stora Coop sänker priserna på 600 av sina mest sålda varor
 med i genomsnitt 6,5% i hela landet. Det är åtminstone ytterligare ett tecken på att konkurrenstrycket i dagligvaruhandeln är högt och ger inget stöd för någon bred ny prisuppgång på livsmedel just nu.

articles.title: Higher home price sentiment
articles.heading: SEB Housing Price Indicator (Sweden)
articles.fulltext:
The SEB Housing Price Indicator rebounded in October, rising by 2 units to 43. Housing market sentiment has been relatively stable so far this year and in October was largely in line with where it was in January. The most recent data suggests that overall consumer confidence has risen above the historical average, closing the spread vs the housing price indicator. The October Housing Price Indicator also reveals a view of rising interest rates triggering a higher share who are planning to fix mortgage rates.
Key points
Home price sentiment rose 
by 
2 index points to 43 in October, almost the same level as at the start of the year, as more respondents expect higher prices
Sentiment has stayed above its historical average for more than a year
Households’ interest rate expectations continue higher, and 15% 
plan
 to fix rates
The housing market sentiment has been relatively stable for a long time and has now remained above the 
historical
 average for more than a year. Hence, as indicated in various other economic sentiment indicators
,
 the strong headwinds from higher energy prices and geopolitics 
do
 not appear to have left a negative mark on economic activity.
Households’ home price 
sentiment has 
for some time been stronger than consumer confidence would imply.
 However, the last consumer confidence reading suggested Swedish households finally becoming more upbeat than the 
historical
 average for the first time since 2021. Consumption data also suggest
s
 stronger activity and the overall impression suggest
s
 a more solid footing for Swedish households. That being said, elevated energy prices are now also affecting all energy consumption and the most recent switch in the prospects for the policy rate add to these headwinds (read more 
here
).
The higher reading in the October indicator was driven by 
the 
share of respondents expecting prices to increase (from 51% in September
 to 53% in October)
,
 while the share expecting prices to decline was unchanged (
as was the share
 expecting prices to be unchanged)
.
In the October survey we see respondents preparing for higher policy rates, but there was also a relatively large change in the share planning to fix mortgage rates. However, since the beginning of July
,
 2y mortgage bond yields have already risen by 70bp, so it remains to be seen what 
those with
 a 3M mortgage rate will do (currently 80% of the stock).

articles.title: Unexpected employment slowdown supports Fed pause in October
articles.heading: US Economy
articles.fulltext:
Payroll employment (NFP) growth slowed to only 29k in September, well below all estimates ahead of the data, and with new large downward revisions to previous months. The unemployment rate increased, reflecting a reversal in the participation rate, and earnings growth slowed. Employment data is notoriously unreliable, but the modest performance according to the new data adds further support to some Fed members’ calls for an October pause. 
Key points
Nonfarm payrolls grew by 29k (estimated 90k, previous 133k, revised from 162k)
Downward revisions of 60k over the past two months
Unemployment rate increased to 4.2% (estimated unchanged at 4.1%)
Labour force participation rate increased to 61.8% (estimated unchanged at 61.6%)
Hourly earnings slowed to 0.1%, 3.0% y/y (estimated unchanged at 0.3%, 3.1%)
Slower employment growth goes against recent signs of accelerating activity but not necessarily a sign of weakness
Support for a Fed pause in October
Volatile data but not sending the same strong signals as before 
US labour market reports is one of the data with most market impact, and one of the hardest to predict, given a large monthly volatility and often substantial revisions. One should therefore be careful to draw conclusions from single months. An unusually low response rate in September is another reason for caution this time. Still, the large downward surprise in September means that we are again back in the “low-hire, low-fire” description of the labour market, with sluggish employment growth but also very low layoffs.
No reason for the Fed to worry about labour market weakness
The Fed has for some time described the labour market as stable and enabling it to focus on the too high inflation. Stricter immigration policies/deportations and an aging population means that the break-even employment growth needed for a stable labour market is lower than before. Thus, the slowdown in job creation in September should not necessarily be seen as a sign of weakness by the Fed. Fed staff in an analysis earlier this year concluded that even months with negative employment changes could become the new normal in this situation. The current 3-month average employment growth of around 50k should be in line with estimates for the new break-even of 30 to 60k per month. The small increase in the unemployment rate should also not be a sign of concern given the volatility in this data and a mostly downward trend this year.
Support for an October Fed pause 
Still, we believe the data should support the views among some influential members of the Fed, vice Chair John Williams and vice Chair Philip Jefferson, that the Fed could take time to evaluate the September hike. The fast employment growth seen in August added to the picture of continued resilient and perhaps even accelerating US growth and has by many in the Fed been seen as a sign that policy is not restrictive enough to bring inflation back to target. That conclusion is less obvious given the slowdown and downward revisions in the September report. 
September employment below all estimates, back to mostly downward revisions
The overall increase in non-farm payrolls at 29k was below the low range in the consensus estimates (35k to 180k) and well below the median estimate (90k). Downward revisions were 60k and we are again back in the pattern with mostly downward revisions.
Non-cyclical employment not the same driver now
Government jobs declined by 17k, after a temporary uptick in September. Private health care and social assistance continue to add jobs but at a slower pace than before (September +23k). Taken together, employment in non-cyclical sectors, which have at times been the key driver for the labour market, was little changed in September (+3k). Employment within cyclical sectors is showing a weakening trend too. Ongoing job losses within especially information (-10k) and financial activities (-7k) could be a sign that AI is affecting some sectors of the economy. The renewed decline in temporary health services (-11k) is a generally weak sign, since this is presumably the category of workers where firms would begin when needing to cut down its work force. Employment within leisure and entertainment has been volatile during summer, perhaps partly reflecting effects of the World Cup, and slowed again in September (+10k).
Higher unemployment rate should alleviate any concerns of overheating
The unemployment rate edged higher again, from 4.1% to 4.2%. This reflects a further recovery in the participation rate, which is normally a sign of strength for the labour market, though this time it follows a steady downward trend during this year. 4.2% is still well in line with the Fed’s view of a stable labour market and a single month’s change should not affect their views much. Still, the upturn should help alleviate any concerns that an increased demand for workers could eventually force companies to pay more to attract workers.
Low earnings growth means that the labour market is not currently an inflation risk 
Earnings growth slowed (0.2% m/m, 3.0% y/y, down from 0.3%/3.1%). Given productivity growth of 2% y/y or more, this should not be a threat to the inflation target. Hourly earnings data in the employment report is not adjusted for changes in the mix of workers and can also be affected by calendar effects depending on the dates in the survey week. We view wages according to the quarterly Employment Cost Index, ECI, as a more reliable measure, but the message from both sources is the same, that the labour market is not a source of inflation at present.
Dovish market reactions
The market reacted by further lowering the probability of an October rate hike to around 20% (5 bp) but continues to fully price a December hike (25 bp accumulated). The market is now pricing a total of three additional rate hikes in 2026 and 2027, after the September increase. We have predicted one more rate increase by the Fed in December, and a return to rate cuts again in late 2027 and see no reason to change these views because of this data.

articles.title: Busy global agenda with Fed and ECB minutes in focus
articles.heading: The Week Ahead
articles.fulltext:
The coming week offers a busy global agenda, with central bank communication and key inflation data in focus. Fed and ECB minutes, together with several ECB speeches, will be closely watched following the recent rise in yields. In Sweden and Norway, September inflation will take centre stage, while the French and Norwegian budgets and EU-China trade talks add to the political agenda.  
US:
Fed minutes will be in focus following the unexpectedly hawkish Fed rate projections, the more hawkish shift in market expectations over the autumn, and the sharp upturn in yields. We will also get more input on service-sector activity from the ISM, following the recent very strong signals from the services PMI.
Euro area: 
Industrial production for major economies will be interesting. Also, German industrial orders can help shed some light on production in the near term. There will be lots of ECB speeches and the ECB will publish its account of Sept. 9-10 policy meeting. Finally, the formal submission of the French budget for 2027 (October 6) and the EU-China trade talks 8-9 October will be important.
Sweden:
September CPI is the main event. Growth indicators for August, service sector PMI, the budget balance, home prices from Mäklarstatistik and our own Housing Price indicator will be of interest this week as well. 
We also keep an eye on the Riksbank Governor Thedéen's speech on Thursday.
Norway:
The government’s budget proposal for 2027 due Wednesday will draw attention this week, and a number of budget measures have been leaked, suggesting increased spending on a broad range of social and defence related posts. Fiscal policy will likely remain somewhat expansionary though to lesser extent than in previous years. Friday’s inflation data for Sep will be of high importance for the market. Norges Bank lowered its near-term forecast by as much as 0.5ppt in its Sep MPR and we see upside risk to its near-term trajectory.

articles.title: An update of current market views
articles.heading: Macro Trading Strategy
articles.fulltext:
FX: Euro view challenged (stuck in a range before weak USD in 2027); short EURCHF overlay starting to play out; short SEK view since April shifted to only play it against JPY (prudent to scale back long EURSEK and NOKSEK)
We had argued a few weeks back in the 
FX Pilot
 that Euro is stuck in a range but probably to test the downside before breaking out higher in 2027
. Risks (France and gas prices) are ‘known knowns’ and should have less broad contagion risk. Clearly 
this story is challenged
 as Euro is breaking levels – we crudely estimated that around 1.10 in EURUSD the CTA type positioning should be max short.
O
ur view has been that playing a longer-term weak USD view in 2027 is best expressed via low delta EURUSD calls given the risks (updated charts below from September FX Pilot).
With that said we argued in September for running a short EURCHF overlay which is starting to play out.
French fiscal issues at risk of spilling over to Euro – should imply EURCHF lower as in 2024/25.
Positive news on Hormuz/oil – helps low yielders, goes against the carry trade (carry strategies are inherently long commodity beta), while positioning is very short CHF. 
Escalation of the oil/negative bond vortex – risks spilling over to equities as in March and imply EURCHF lower.
Meanwhile – SNB is de facto easing policy by allowing the real policy rate to drift into negative territory while the REER is depreciating – i.e. they could allow FX to do some of the tightening here.
On 
Monday
 this week we dialled back negativity on SEK vs European crosses (EUR and NOK) – but keep short SEKJPY.
SEK is very short positioned (like CHF) with the risk that French issues spill over to Euro while the gas price support for NOK should start stalling during October near peak EU ‘restocking’. I.e. it looked prudent to scale back SEK short views vs Euro and NOK as short covering could take hold.
With that said, sticking with a view of short SEKJPY (& CADJPY) – as a carry efficient way to play long Yen while having some ‘protection’ for a 2022 redux. Should a clear energy price disinflation impulse emerge look to only express long Yen vs CAD and USD. 
Interest Rates: Playing the Fixed Income bear market via ‘Macro RV’ implementations in NOK (AUD) and SEK:
I have certainly been directionally wrong, thinking we were priced for sticky inflation about 40bps ago …
Three thematic drivers have coincided with algo positioning getting to an extreme short position in longer bond futures - the themes being:
AI crowding out bonds both via equities attracting capital (foreign net purchases of US securities has entirely pivoted to equities from US treasuries) and corporate debt issuance.
Decent growth backdrop (AI capex driven) and a geopolitical inflation impulse.
Japan capital outflows stalling and possibly reversing.
Currently these themes and positioning (discussed above) are coinciding for a ‘peak bond crisis’ – question is where the narrative can change ahead?
The obvious one is that we get some progress on opening Hormuz – allowing for carbon molecules to flow freely but also importantly releasing shipping capacity/reducing transfer costs. This seems unlikely in the coming month ahead of US midterms.
Otherwise, the bond market needs the ‘automatic stabilizer’ to kick-in, i.e. equity markets to correct/a dent in the AI theme (or global PMIs to roll over). Markets are certainly trading as if the bond sell-off won’t stop until equities take a hit.
We have taken a very nitty gritty/defensive view of how to play the rates sell-off via positioning for front FRA-spread steepening in Norway (equivalent could have been done in Australia) 
– more in Norway 360 publications 
here
:
The high yielders (Norway and Australia) have had distinct curve shapes as they seem closer to a peak in the hiking cycle with very front FRA spreads having traded below/near zero (e.g. Dec26/March27). 
As long as these central banks can be seen as not cutting rates within 6 months these micro steepeners are essentially cheap optionality on hiking cycles having to be extended further. This has worked in Australia in particular but there should be more potential in Norway, looking for Dec26/March27 spread to get to 12bps (right chart below). 
In the coming weeks one will have to assess whether to extend micro steepening to March27/June27 if it trades below zero.
Norway and Australia are arguably running restrictive policy which should justify curve inversion into the belly. 
In Norway we opted (too early) for a view of June27/June28 inversion – this still looks like an interesting expression in both Norway and Australia though. 
Combined with the very front steepener view (discussed above) one essentially ends up with an implicit fly expression, e.g. pay belly of Dec26/June27/June28.
In Sweden we have opted to play long SGBs on ASW as a catch-up to the move higher in yields & a risk-off hedge while fading the pricing for Riksbank hikes on spread to Europe in 1Y1Y 
– more in Sweden 360 publications 
here
.
The SGB ASW trades directionally with yields but lagged the initial move higher in rates – 
i.e. there was a good case for a bid returning for bonds at attractive levels while also providing a ‘risk-off’ implementation.
 This trade has now blown past our take profit target.
Received 1Y1Y Stibor vs ESTR 
has had a correction lower again with the dislocation in European rate markets, making it interesting to replay the substantial Riksbank/ECB convergence priced.

articles.title: Elevated core inflation, but big test still ahead of us
articles.heading: Euro area inflation
articles.fulltext:
Both headline and core HICP remain elevated, but core inflation has moved broadly sideways for most of 2026. We continue to see little evidence of adverse spillovers from elevated energy prices, and the rise in core goods prices are attributed to other driving forces. The big test for projections when it comes to indirect effects due to high energy prices still lies ahead of us.
September HICP 3.8% y/y (SEB 3.5%, cons. 3.7%) and core HICP 2.5% y/y (SEB 2.4%, cons. 2.5%).
Key points
Broader energy prices key driver, little evidence of spillovers
The longer trend of higher core goods prices continues
Perhaps the first sign of rising food prices.
Elevated headline and core but still in line with the ECB staff projections
The October inflation report confirms the trends shown in previous national wide data releases. Headline HICP continues rising as high energy prices now have broadened from fuel to home energy prices like natural gas and electricity. As was the case in 2021/2022 contract structure and methodology differences will widen the spread from a cross-country perspective.
More importantly, core inflation remains elevated but in the past few months it has been more of a sideways movement, averaging around 2.4%. The October readings for both headline and core HICP are in line with the ECB Staff projections from September.
The 2026 core trend continues
While core inflation has moved roughly sideways in 2026 the underlying trend has been gradually higher 
for
 core goods prices while there has been a softening of the elevated service prices. While the latter is due to somewhat softer demand and wages, the former is partly explained by a trend of higher ICT and medicine prices, a trend which started already at the beginning of this year. 
We would also like to remind readers that service prices have been erratic over the past few years. Our impression is that this partly reflects changes in the seasonal pattern, and we have therefore preferred to assess the full set of August-November period before drawing any firm conclusions. The decline in September service prices this year was less than in the past few years but in the lower range taken by a longer historic metric. Hence, we await details to give more insight into this.
Test of spillovers still ahead of us
The key issue from a monetary policy perspective is any adverse spillovers from higher energy prices to a broader range of prices. These indirect effects normally happen with an extensive time lag. We and the ECB have the same profile for these indirect effects, and they start appearing by the end of this year and mostly during H1 2027. Hence, the test for how strong this effect will be is still ahead of us. Hence, up until October the narrative of little evidence of indirect effects remains.
Food prices are still on the soft side
During the September ECB Press conference, President Lagarde highlighted that the ECB had been surprised by developments in food prices. It is plausible that unprocessed food prices would respond more quickly to high energy prices and other supply-side disruptions. However, after several years of declining global food prices, the downward pressure on consumer prices appears to have been stronger—or it may still be a question of timing.
We continue to see relatively subdued food price developments, although we acknowledge the relatively large rise in unprocessed food prices in Italy. Indeed, the euro area as a whole recorded its first increase in overall food prices since April, driven by unprocessed food prices.
No policy implications
The October inflation figures are in line with the ECB staff projections, and we continue to see little evidence of significant spillovers. We therefore do not expect today’s figures alone to change the ECB’s assessment, and we continue to expect the next rate hike in December.
